column2: His sons and friends are to be fined a pana each; then they should perform the expiation prescribed by the scriptures.
Those who die by water, fire or hanging, who fall from renunciation or from a fast, who perish by poison or a fall, or are killed by weapons,
and who are not settled in renunciation and are cast out by all the world, are purified by the Chandrayana, or by two Taptakrichchhra penances.
One who has fallen from both (states), a sinner fallen from the black-and-spotted vow, is purified by two Chandrayanas and by giving a cow and a bull.
One touched by dogs, jackals, monkeys and the like, or by people (impure), without sexual contact, is purified at once by bathing, by day, at the twilights, or at night.
One who unknowingly eats a Chandala's food in any way is purified in half a month, living on cow's urine and barley gruel.
One who burns the house of a cow or Brahmin, or causes death by hanging and the like, or cuts a noose — the twice-born should perform one Krichchhra penance.
One who eats food of Chandalas and Pulkasas, or kills a woman, should perform half a Krichchhra, knowingly; unknowingly, two Chandrayanas.
Those who eat the food of Kapalikas, go to their women, or have forbidden intercourse, a Brahmin who drinks liquor or eats meat,
after the Taptakrichchhra is purified by the Maurvi oblation. Especially the four who commit great sins
are purified by entering fire, or by standing in a great sacrifice. One who has done a secret sin is likewise (purified) by practice for a month,
or by reciting the Aghamarshana hymn while standing in water. Washermen, leather-workers, actors, basket-weavers,
fishermen, Medas and Bhillas — these seven are remembered as the lowest-born. One who eats their food, goes to their women, drinks, or accepts a gift from them
should do half a Krichchhra knowingly, and two Chandrayanas unknowingly. One who has intercourse with his mother, his teacher's wife, daughter, sister or daughter-in-law
should enter fire; no other purification is prescribed. One who has gone to a queen, a female ascetic, a nurse, or a woman of higher class
should do two Krichchhras; and the same for a woman of the same gotra. With these, women of the father's gotra and the mother's gotra,
and with all women of one's family, a half-Krichchhra penance is to be done. For going to a prostitute, Brahmins remove the sin
by drinking, once, for five nights, kusha water mixed with... The Brahmin who has violated his teacher's bed should do the vow as prescribed.
Some desire (a penance) for killing a cow, and others for the "avakirni"; one who strikes down a cow with a blow above the staff,
his penance is the cow-vow doubled. The staff for cows is declared thumb-thick, arm-long,
moist and with leaves. And if a cow dies and a calf is in her womb,
each one should be expiated with a Krichchhra; this is the expiation for killing a cow. In binding, restraining, or feeding cows in sickness,
if death occurs, he is not touched by blame; if she falls in a faint and is struck by a staff,
and after rising walks six or fifteen steps, or takes a mouthful of food, or drinks water,
for the death of one lost to any disease there is no expiation. If cows are killed by sticks, clods, stones or weapons,
the penance is: by weapon one thing; by wood the Santapana; by a clod the Prajapatya;
by a stone the Taptakrichchhra; by a weapon the Atikrichchhra. He should give medicine, oil and food to the cow and Brahmins.
If death occurs while giving them, then there is no penance. For drinking oil or medicine, or eating medicines,
or removing a thorn, there is no penance; also for tying calves by the neck, or treating them,
or keeping them at evening for protection, there is no fault, nor in anger or binding. At a quarter, the hair; at a half, only the beard;
at three-quarters, the topknot; at the full, everything. He should have all hair removed, cutting two finger-breadths.
So too for women, shaving of the head is declared (as a cutting of hair); a woman should not be shaved, nor sit in the hero's posture.
She should not dwell in the cow-pen, nor follow a cow that is going. King, king's son-killer, or a much-learned Brahmin:
without shaving them a penance may be prescribed; to protect their hair, a doubled vow is ordained.
When the doubled vow has been completed, the fee for the vow is doubled.
The killer's sin is not destroyed, and the giver goes to hell, in those who declare a penance not prescribed by Vedic or Smriti texts.
The king should punish such obstructers of dharma with a fine; and the king should not, in any case, oppress them out of desire or confusion.
That sin, becoming a hundredfold, pursues him. After the expiation is done, he should feed Brahmins,
and give twenty cows and a bull as their fee. For worms born of grass, or flies and the like falling in,
one should do half a Krichchhra and give a fee according to ability. Having done penance and fed the best of Brahmins,
he should give a gold mana; then purification is ordained. If touched by Chandalas or Shvapachas at night, bathing is prescribed;
one should not stay there at night; he is purified at once by bathing. If a fool stays there at night unknowingly,
then that sin of his becomes a hundredfold. When stars rise, or planets above, and their rays touch (one),
he should bathe in water. And earths from water, anthills, mouse-holes, thoroughfares,
cremation grounds, or left from cleansing are not to be taken. The Brahmin should carefully perform "ishta" and "purta".
By ishta he gains heaven, by purta liberation. Ishta is spending wealth in sacrifice; purta is said to be a tank,
and especially gardens, temple tanks, wells, ponds, and temples.
He who restores those fallen into ruin gets the former fruit. From a white cow one takes urine; from a black cow, dung;
from a copper-coloured cow, milk; from a white one, curd; from a tawny cow, ghee — destroying great sins.
Taking each substance separately with kusha and water from holy places and rivers, raising it with "Om",
stirring with "Om", one should drink with "Om", in a vessel of palasha leaf, middle leaf, or auspicious copper vessel;
or one drinks kusha water from a lotus leaf or clay vessel. When birth-impurity occurs and a second arises,
there is no fault in the second; he is purified by the first. By a birth, a birth; by a death, a death.
In a miscarriage in the month, three days are prescribed.
In miscarriage, one is purified in nights equal to the months. A chaste woman at the end of her menses is purified by bathing.
A woman falls from her own gotra at the seventh step of marriage; the rites of rice-balls and water are to be done for her in her husband's gotra.
In giving rice-balls, the intended recipients are named; in each ball two names; three balls for six; thus the giver is not confused.
A mother enjoys with her husband for a thousand years, divinely; the grandmother with hers, and the great-grandmother with hers.
In the year, one should honour mother and father; he should feed Brahmins at a shraddha without the gods' rite and offer a single ball.
Shraddha is known by the wise as fivefold: daily, occasional, desire-motivated, for increase (vriddhi), and at parvan.
At eclipses, on solstices, at festivals and at temples, a man offers three balls; on the day of death, a single one.
An unmarried girl is not separate in ball, gotra or impurity; by the marriage mantras she falls from her own gotra.
Whatever class a girl is married into, the impurity and the rice-ball and water rites are equal to that class.
When the marriage is completed, on the fourth day and night she becomes one with her husband in ball, gotra and impurity.
On the first, second, third or fourth day, the collecting of bones should be done by kinsmen with kind intent.
On the fourth, fifth, seventh and ninth day, the collecting of bones is declared for the classes in order.
He for whom a bull is released on the eleventh day after death is freed from the world of the dead and honoured in heaven.
Standing in water to the navel, one should think in the heart: "May my ancestors come and take these handfuls of water."
Joining the hands and filling them with water, lifting it to the height of a cow's horn, he should pour it into the water.
Standing in water, facing south, he should cast water to the sky; the sky and the south direction are the place of the ancestors.
Waters are said to be the hosts of gods, and waters are the hosts of ancestors; therefore water should be given by one wishing the ancestors' good.
Water warmed by the sun's rays by day, by stars and winds by night, and by both between, is always pure.
Water of its natural state, unmanifest, never defiled by impurity, whether in a vessel or on the ground, is always pure.
One should give handfuls of water to the gods and ancestors; for those who died without rites, the wise should give on the ground.
At a shraddha and at the time of oblation one gives with one hand; in tarpana with both: this rule is fixed.
